case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Double Jeopardy Clause prohibits cumulative sentences for separate convictions under 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) and § 924(j) when both arise from the same underlying criminal conduct.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Fifth Amendment Double Jeopardy Clause; 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(A) (using a firearm during a crime of violence); 18 U.S.C. § 924(j) (murder using a firearm during a crime of violence); 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) consecutive sentencing provisions
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Dwayne Barrett, supported by both his defense counsel and notably the U.S. Solicitor General, argues that § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j), triggering a presumption under the Double Jeopardy Clause against cumulative punishments. Because Congress did not include explicit language in § 924(j) authorizing cumulative sentences on top of § 924(c) penalties — unlike other provisions where Congress expressly authorized stacked punishments — the presumption against cumulative punishment should stand unrebutted. The selective use of cumulative-punishment language elsewhere in § 924(c) demonstrates that Congress's silence regarding §§ 924(c) and 924(j) was intentional and meaningful.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Court-appointed amicus, defending the Second Circuit's judgment below, argues that cumulative sentences under §§ 924(c) and 924(j) are permissible. Amicus contends that § 924(c)'s statutory minimums and consecutive-sentencing requirements reflect congressional intent to impose separate, stacked punishments. Amicus further argues that the absence of cumulative-punishment language in § 924(j) is not dispositive, citing Missouri v. Hunter, where the Supreme Court found clear legislative intent for cumulative punishment even though only one of two statutes contained explicit cumulative-sentencing language. Amicus also argues that because Congress enacted § 924(j) long after § 924(c) was established, it legislated against the backdrop of § 924(c)'s consecutive-sentencing mandate, implying awareness and acceptance of cumulative punishment.
key_precedents: Missouri v. Hunter, 459 U.S. 359 (1983) — established that cumulative punishments are permissible under the Double Jeopardy Clause when the legislature clearly intends them, even if only one statute contains explicit cumulative-punishment language
Blockburger v. United States — foundational lesser-included offense test used to determine whether two offenses are the 'same offense' for Double Jeopardy purposes
Delligatti v. United States, No. 23-825 — pending Supreme Court case on 'crime of violence' definition under § 924(c), argued to potentially clarify governing legal principles relevant to Barrett
Flowers v. Mississippi, 136 S. Ct. 2157 (2016) — cited for the standard governing GVR (grant, vacate, remand) practice when a pending ruling may alter the legal landscape

Garland v. Range, No. 23-374 — cited by petitioner for the government's own prior acknowledgment that a pending ruling justifying a hold need not definitively resolve the question but must shed substantial light on the proper analysis
United States v. Barrett, 102 F.4th 60 (2d Cir. 2024) — the Second Circuit decision under review, which upheld cumulative sentencing under §§ 924(c) and 924(j)
United States v. Barrett, 937 F.3d 126 (2d Cir.) — prior Second Circuit proceeding in the same case
United States v. Barrett, 903 F.3d 166 (2d Cir.) — earlier Second Circuit proceeding in the same case
case_analysis.legal_complexity: Complex — The case involves the intersection of Double Jeopardy doctrine, statutory construction of overlapping federal firearm statutes, lesser-included offense analysis, and competing interpretive frameworks regarding congressional silence versus express authorization of cumulative punishments. The unusual procedural posture — where the United States Solicitor General filed a brief supporting the petitioner against the government's own prior litigation position, necessitating appointment of independent amicus curiae to defend the judgment below — adds significant institutional and jurisprudential complexity. The case also implicates potential interactions with a separate pending Supreme Court ruling in Delligatti, further layering the legal analysis.

John Roberts.reasoning: The conference has achieved genuine unanimity grounded in sound legal reasoning rather than mere consensus-seeking, and I am satisfied that the narrow textual holding I outlined in my prior reasoning remains the correct and appropriately limited ground for decision. Justice Barrett's articulation of the canon of meaningful variation — that Congress's use of 'in addition to' in § 924(c)(1)(A) while omitting any such language in § 924(j) is an affirmative textual signal, not mere silence — is the strongest formulation of the core argument and one I would adopt in the majority opinion. Justice Kagan's point that the 'statutory backdrop' theory would swallow the Blockburger presumption entirely is the decisive response to the respondent's strongest counterargument, and I would make that the centerpiece of the opinion's analytical work. As Chief Justice, I will assign the majority opinion to myself and write narrowly: the holding should rest solely on the intra-statutory textual contrast within § 924 itself, avoiding broad pronouncements about Double Jeopardy doctrine that could unsettle other statutory schemes, and expressly reserving the question of how Missouri v. Hunter applies where Congress has not provided the same kind of affirmative intra-statutory contrast present here.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: My colleagues have collectively reinforced the core textualist analysis I find most compelling: Congress's deliberate deployment of 'in addition to' cumulative-punishment language in § 924(c)(1)(A) while conspicuously omitting any such language in § 924(j) is the dispositive textual signal under Missouri v. Hunter. Justice Gorsuch correctly observes that Hunter itself turned on express statutory language requiring punishment 'in addition to' the predicate crime — precisely what is absent from § 924(j) — which means the amicus's reliance on Hunter actually undermines the respondent's position rather than supporting it. Justice Barrett's point about the canon of meaningful variation is particularly well-taken from an originalist-textualist standpoint: when Congress drafts two provisions within the same statutory scheme and includes cumulative-punishment authorization in one but not the other, that structural contrast is not inadvertent but reflects a deliberate legislative choice we are bound to respect. The Solicitor General's concession further confirms that no serious textual argument sustains cumulative punishment here, and the rule of lenity resolves any residual ambiguity in the defendant's favor.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The conference unanimity across sharply different methodological approaches — from Justice Thomas's originalist textualism to Justice Sotomayor's purposivist concern for defendants' rights to Justice Kagan's pragmatic textualism — confirms that the textual and structural case here is genuinely strong rather than merely plausible. I continue to find Justice Thomas's intra-statutory contrast argument most compelling under my own textualist methodology: Congress's deliberate use of 'in addition to' cumulative-punishment language in § 924(c)(1)(A) while omitting any such language in § 924(j) is not mere silence but an affirmative signal under the canon of meaningful variation, and Missouri v. Hunter's 'clear legislative intent' standard cannot be satisfied by inference from statutory backdrop alone. The strongest counterargument — that § 924(j) was enacted against the backdrop of § 924(c)'s consecutive-sentencing framework and therefore implicitly incorporated it — fails precisely because, as Justice Kagan correctly identifies, accepting that logic would render the Blockburger presumption a nullity whenever a later statute overlaps with an earlier mandatory-minimum scheme, which cannot be what Hunter intended. I write separately to emphasize that while I agree with the outcome, the holding should rest firmly on textual and structural grounds rather than the rule of lenity, which should remain a genuine last resort rather than a convenient shortcut when the text itself provides the answer.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I find myself in strong agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself is telling — when Justice Thomas and I reach the same conclusion through different methodological paths, the legal foundation is particularly solid. Justice Barrett's point about the canon of meaningful variation is especially compelling: Congress demonstrated in § 924(c)(1)(A) that it knows precisely how to authorize cumulative punishment with 'in addition to' language, and its deliberate omission of any such language in § 924(j) cannot be dismissed as inadvertent drafting. The strongest argument for the Respondent would be the Missouri v. Hunter backdrop theory — that Congress legislated § 924(j) knowing § 924(c)'s consecutive-sentencing framework existed — but as Justice Kagan correctly observes, accepting that logic would effectively swallow the Blockburger presumption entirely whenever a later statute overlaps with an earlier mandatory-minimum scheme. From my perspective, the real-world stakes for defendants like Dwayne Barrett — facing dramatically harsher sentences based on congressional ambiguity — combined with the rule of lenity and the Solicitor General's own concession, make the case for the petitioner overwhelming, and I write separately to emphasize that the Double Jeopardy Clause's protection of human dignity demands we not permit cumulative punishment absent unmistakably clear congressional authorization.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett have both sharpened the core textual argument in ways I find persuasive and consistent with my own pragmatic textualism: the intra-statutory contrast within § 924 itself is not merely an argument from silence but an affirmative signal, because Congress demonstrated in § 924(c)(1)(A) that it knows precisely how to authorize cumulative punishment with 'in addition to' language, and its deliberate omission of any such language in § 924(j) — enacted years later with full awareness of § 924(c)'s framework — is the most coherent textual signal available. The strongest argument from the amicus's position is that Congress legislated § 924(j) against the backdrop of § 924(c)'s mandatory consecutive-sentencing structure, but as Justice Sotomayor correctly notes, the 1994 legislative history actually cuts the other way — Congress rejected a proposal that would have explicitly integrated § 924(j) into § 924(c)'s cumulative framework, which is about as clear a negative legislative signal as one can find. Under Missouri v. Hunter, the clarity required to rebut Blockburger must be discernible from the statutory text or legislative history, and here both sources point in the same direction: no cumulative punishment was authorized. The unanimity of my colleagues on this point, while not determinative, reflects that the textual and structural case is genuinely strong rather than merely plausible.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The conference has reached remarkable unanimity, and reviewing my colleagues' arguments only strengthens my conviction. Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett both sharpen the critical textualist point I find most compelling: Congress's intra-statutory contrast between § 924(c)'s explicit 'in addition to' cumulative-punishment language and § 924(j)'s conspicuous silence is not mere inadvertence but a deliberate drafting choice that must be given effect under the canon of meaningful variation. The amicus's strongest counterargument — that Congress legislated § 924(j) against the backdrop of § 924(c)'s consecutive-sentencing mandate — is precisely what Justice Kagan correctly identifies as proving too much: accepting that logic would effectively swallow the Blockburger presumption whenever a later statute overlaps with an earlier one carrying mandatory consecutive sentences, rendering the Double Jeopardy protection a nullity in the modern sentencing enhancement context. Missouri v. Hunter requires clear legislative intent for cumulative punishment, and when Congress has demonstrated in the very same statutory scheme that it knows how to express such intent explicitly, its failure to do so in § 924(j) is the clearest possible signal — reinforced by the rule of lenity — that stacking these two penalties was not authorized.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The conference's unanimity across sharply divergent methodological approaches — from Justice Thomas's strict textualism to Justice Sotomayor's defendant-centered analysis to Justice Kagan's pragmatic textualism — confirms that the core holding rests on genuinely solid ground rather than mere coalition-building. I am particularly persuaded by Justice Kagan's identification of the 1994 legislative history, which Justice Jackson also emphasizes: Congress's affirmative rejection of a proposal that would have explicitly integrated § 924(j) into § 924(c)'s cumulative framework is not merely negative inference but an affirmative legislative signal that the 'statutory backdrop' theory cannot overcome. The strongest remaining argument for the respondent — that § 924(j) was enacted with full awareness of § 924(c)'s consecutive-sentencing structure and therefore implicitly incorporated it — fails precisely because Missouri v. Hunter demands clarity, and when Congress has demonstrated in the same statute that it knows how to authorize cumulative punishment expressly, its failure to do so is the clearest available signal of contrary intent. Consistent with Chief Justice Roberts's instinct toward institutional restraint, I would join a narrow opinion grounded in the specific intra-statutory textual contrast, avoiding broad Double Jeopardy pronouncements that could unsettle other statutory schemes.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The conference has reached genuine unanimity through multiple independent methodological paths, which strengthens rather than merely confirms my position. Justice Kagan's identification of the 1994 legislative history — Congress's rejection of a proposal that would have explicitly integrated § 924(j) into § 924(c)'s cumulative framework — is a significant addition to the textual analysis I had already found compelling, because it transforms what might otherwise appear as mere statutory silence into affirmative negative legislative intent. The strongest remaining counterargument is the 'statutory backdrop' theory, but as I noted in my prior reasoning and as Justice Alito correctly emphasizes, background context cannot supply the 'clear' legislative intent that Missouri v. Hunter demands when the foreground text — specifically the intra-statutory contrast between § 924(c)'s explicit 'in addition to' language and § 924(j)'s conspicuous omission — affirmatively signals a different congressional choice. I would write to ground the holding narrowly in the canon of meaningful variation as applied to this specific intra-statutory contrast, reserving broader Double Jeopardy pronouncements for cases that actually require them, consistent with Chief Justice Roberts's prudential instinct to avoid unsettling other statutory schemes.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I find myself in strong agreement with Justice Sotomayor's observation that the 1994 legislative history — specifically Congress's rejection of a proposal that would have explicitly placed § 924(j) within § 924(c)'s cumulative-punishment framework — is particularly powerful evidence that the silence in § 924(j) was deliberate rather than inadvertent. Justice Thomas's textualist point about intra-statutory contrast also resonates with my own methodology: when Congress uses explicit 'in addition to' language in § 924(c) but omits it entirely from § 924(j), that structural contrast within the same statutory scheme affirmatively cuts against cumulative punishment rather than merely leaving the question open. The strongest argument from the respondent's side — that Congress legislated § 924(j) against the backdrop of § 924(c)'s consecutive-sentencing mandate — fails because, as Justice Kagan correctly notes, that logic would effectively swallow the Blockburger presumption in any case involving overlapping statutes with mandatory minimums, rendering the Double Jeopardy protection meaningless. My background as a public defender makes me acutely aware that the practical consequence of stacking these penalties falls hardest on defendants who face dramatically disproportionate sentences based on congressional ambiguity that the rule of lenity and the Double Jeopardy Clause were designed to resolve in their favor.

John Roberts.reasoning: Applying Blockburger's lesser-included offense test, § 924(c)(1)(A) is facially subsumed within § 924(j), which requires all elements of § 924(c) plus the additional element of murder — triggering the presumption against cumulative punishment. While Missouri v. Hunter permits cumulative sentences when legislative intent is clear from the face of the statute or legislative history, the critical distinction here is that Congress expressly included cumulative-punishment and consecutive-sentencing language in § 924(c) itself but conspicuously omitted any such authorization in § 924(j), and the canon of expressio unius counsels that this silence is meaningful rather than inadvertent. The amicus's reliance on the statutory backdrop argument — that Congress legislated § 924(j) against the existing § 924(c) framework — is insufficient under Whalen v. United States, which required that cumulative punishment be 'elsewhere specially authorized by Congress,' not merely inferrable from legislative context. Consistent with my preference for narrow, institutionally cautious rulings, I would hold that absent clear textual authorization in § 924(j) for stacking penalties on top of § 924(c), the Double Jeopardy Clause's presumption against cumulative punishment stands unrebutted, and one conviction must be vacated per Ball v. United States.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Applying textualist and originalist principles, the Double Jeopardy Clause's original public meaning prohibited multiple punishments for the same offense, and the Blockburger lesser-included offense analysis confirms that § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) since every element of § 924(c) is subsumed within § 924(j). While Missouri v. Hunter correctly recognizes that Congress may authorize cumulative punishments, that authorization must be discernible from the statutory text itself — and critically, Congress expressly included cumulative-punishment language in § 924(c)(1)(A) stating punishment is 'in addition to' the predicate offense penalty, yet included no such language in § 924(j). Under basic textualist canons, this deliberate omission is meaningful: Congress knew how to authorize stacked punishments explicitly, did so elsewhere in the very same statutory scheme, and chose not to do so in § 924(j), which is the strongest textual signal that cumulative punishment under both provisions was not authorized. The amicus's reliance on Hunter is misplaced because Hunter involved discerning intent from the broader statutory context, but here the intra-statutory contrast between § 924(c) and § 924(j) affirmatively cuts against cumulative punishment rather than merely remaining silent.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Applying the Blockburger lesser-included offense test, § 924(c)(1)(A) is plainly a lesser-included offense of § 924(j), which requires every element of § 924(c) plus the additional element of murder, triggering the Double Jeopardy presumption against cumulative punishment. Under Missouri v. Hunter, that presumption can be rebutted only by clear legislative intent for cumulative punishment, but unlike § 924(c) itself — which contains explicit 'in addition to' and consecutive-sentencing language — § 924(j) is conspicuously silent on cumulative punishment, and Congress's selective use of such language elsewhere in the same statutory scheme is a meaningful textual signal under basic principles of textualism. The amicus's reliance on Hunter is misplaced because Hunter involved a situation where one statute's explicit language supplied the requisite clarity for the entire statutory scheme; here, § 924(c)'s consecutive-sentencing mandate was designed to stack § 924(c) penalties on top of the underlying predicate offense, not to authorize stacking a § 924(c) penalty on top of a § 924(j) conviction that already subsumes the § 924(c) conduct. Even accounting for law enforcement interests in robust sentencing, the structural and textual evidence does not rise to the level of 'clear legislative intent' Hunter demands when the lesser offense is wholly contained within the greater.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Blockburger v. United States, § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) because every element required to prove § 924(c) — using a firearm during a crime of violence — is necessarily subsumed within § 924(j), which additionally requires that the firearm use result in murder. Where two offenses fail the Blockburger test, the Double Jeopardy Clause raises a strong presumption against cumulative punishment, and that presumption can only be rebutted by clear congressional intent to authorize stacked sentences. Here, Congress's deliberate choice in 1994 to reject a proposal that would have explicitly placed § 924(j) within § 924(c) and authorized 'in addition to' punishment — combined with the absence of any cumulative-sentencing language in § 924(j) comparable to what Congress employed elsewhere in § 924(c) — demonstrates that the silence was intentional, not inadvertent, and the presumption against cumulative punishment stands unrebutted. The fact that even the Solicitor General has abandoned the government's prior litigation position reinforces that the Second Circuit's judgment cannot be sustained, and the practical reality that Dwayne Barrett faces a dramatically harsher sentence based on Congress's ambiguous statutory architecture counsels strongly in favor of the rule of lenity and the constitutional protection the Double Jeopardy Clause was designed to provide.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The textual architecture of § 924 is dispositive here. Congress demonstrated it knows how to authorize cumulative punishments explicitly — it did so in specific subsections of § 924(c) — yet § 924(j) contains no such authorization for stacking penalties on top of a § 924(c) conviction. Under Missouri v. Hunter, the inquiry is whether legislative intent to impose cumulative punishment is 'clear,' and that clarity must emerge from the statutory text or legislative history; mere silence cannot rebut the Blockburger presumption when Congress has shown elsewhere in the very same statutory provision that it uses express language when it wants cumulative punishment. The amicus's argument that Congress legislated § 924(j) against the backdrop of § 924(c)'s consecutive-sentencing mandate proves too much — that logic would swallow the Blockburger presumption entirely in any case where a later statute overlaps with an earlier one carrying mandatory consecutive sentences. As a pragmatic textualist, I find the contrasting textual approaches within § 924 itself to be the most coherent and workable interpretive signal, and the Solicitor General's concession on this point, while unusual, reflects a sound reading of the statute's internal logic.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Applying the Blockburger test as a tool of statutory construction, § 924(c) is plainly a lesser-included offense of § 924(j), which triggers the presumption against cumulative punishment under the Double Jeopardy Clause. The critical textualist question under Missouri v. Hunter is whether Congress clearly expressed intent to rebut that presumption, and the statutory text answers that question decisively: § 924(c)(1)(A) contains explicit 'in addition to' language authorizing stacked punishment atop the predicate offense, but § 924(j) contains no analogous language authorizing additional punishment atop § 924(c). Congress's selective deployment of cumulative-punishment language elsewhere in the same statutory scheme — a drafting choice I must presume was deliberate — is the strongest evidence of legislative intent available, and the rule of lenity further counsels that any remaining ambiguity must be resolved in the defendant's favor. The amicus's reliance on Missouri v. Hunter actually undermines the respondent's position, because Hunter itself turned on express statutory language requiring punishment 'in addition to' the predicate crime, precisely the kind of language absent from § 924(j).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Blockburger, § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j), triggering the presumption against cumulative punishment that can only be rebutted by clear legislative intent. Missouri v. Hunter permits cumulative sentences when legislative intent is clear, but here that clarity is absent — Congress conspicuously omitted from § 924(j) the 'in addition to' cumulative-punishment language it routinely employs elsewhere in § 924(c) and related statutes, and the legislative history of § 924(j) contains no comparable floor statements or explicit references to stacked penalties. The amicus's argument that Congress legislated § 924(j) against the backdrop of § 924(c)'s consecutive-sentencing mandate is plausible but insufficient to constitute the 'clear' legislative intent Hunter requires, particularly when the Solicitor General — the government's own voice — concedes the point against its prior litigation position, a significant institutional signal I take seriously. Applying the principle of judicial restraint and the canon that ambiguity in criminal statutes should be resolved in favor of the defendant, the Blockburger presumption stands unrebutted and cumulative punishment is impermissible.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Applying the Blockburger lesser-included offense test, § 924(c)(1)(A) is plainly a lesser-included offense of § 924(j), which requires every element of § 924(c) plus the additional element of murder — triggering the Double Jeopardy presumption against cumulative punishment. Under Missouri v. Hunter, that presumption can be rebutted only by clear legislative intent, but the textual evidence here cuts against the government: Congress expressly included a 'in addition to the punishment provided' proviso in § 924(c)(1)(A) to authorize cumulative punishment atop predicate offense sentences, yet enacted § 924(j) without any analogous language, and the canon of meaningful variation counsels that this deliberate omission signals Congress did not intend stacked punishments between these two provisions. The amicus's reliance on Hunter is misplaced because in Hunter one of the two statutes contained explicit cumulative-punishment language directed at the other offense, whereas here neither § 924(j) nor its relationship to § 924(c) contains such express authorization — and the Solicitor General's own concession that the statutory backdrop argument proves too much reinforces that congressional silence in § 924(j) is not mere inadvertence but a meaningful textual signal. Consistent with Whalen v. United States and the principle that the Double Jeopardy Clause protects against duplicative convictions and not merely duplicative sentences, the § 924(c) conviction must be vacated.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Under Blockburger, § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j) because every element of § 924(c) is subsumed within § 924(j), which adds only the murder element — triggering the Double Jeopardy presumption against cumulative punishment. While Missouri v. Hunter permits cumulative sentences when Congress clearly intends them, the research confirms that this inquiry requires examining 'language, structure, and legislative history' of the entire statutory scheme, and here Congress's selective use of explicit cumulative-punishment language elsewhere in § 924(c) — combined with its silence in § 924(j) — is powerful structural evidence that Congress did not intend stacking. The amicus's argument that Congress legislated § 924(j) against the backdrop of § 924(c)'s consecutive-sentencing mandate proves too much; that logic would effectively nullify the Double Jeopardy presumption whenever a later statute is enacted in proximity to an existing one with mandatory minimums. As a former public defender acutely aware of how cumulative sentencing produces disproportionate outcomes, I find that the government's own Solicitor General's concession that the presumption is unrebutted here carries significant weight in confirming that no clear legislative intent to stack these particular penalties has been demonstrated.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Double Jeopardy Clause prohibits cumulative sentences for separate convictions under 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) and § 924(j) when both arise from the same underlying criminal conduct.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Fifth Amendment Double Jeopardy Clause; 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(1)(A) (using a firearm during a crime of violence); 18 U.S.C. § 924(j) (murder using a firearm during a crime of violence); 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) consecutive sentencing provisions
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Dwayne Barrett, supported by both the Federal Defenders of New York and — unusually — the U.S. Solicitor General, argues that § 924(c)(1)(A) is a lesser-included offense of § 924(j), triggering a presumption under the Double Jeopardy Clause against cumulative punishments. Because Congress did not include explicit language in § 924(j) authorizing cumulative sentences on top of a § 924(c) conviction, and because Congress selectively authorized cumulative punishments only for certain offenses within § 924(c), no clear congressional intent exists to rebut that presumption. Therefore, imposing consecutive sentences for both offenses based on identical conduct constitutes an unconstitutional double punishment.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Court-appointed amicus curiae (Williams & Connolly LLP), defending the Second Circuit's judgment below, argues that cumulative punishments are permissible because: (1) § 924(c)'s mandatory minimum sentencing structure and consecutive-sentencing requirements demonstrate congressional intent to stack penalties; (2) the absence of explicit cumulative-punishment language in § 924(j) does not preclude such punishment, as established in Missouri v. Hunter, where only one statute contained cumulative-punishment language yet the Court upheld stacked sentences; (3) § 924(j) was enacted against the backdrop of § 924(c)'s already-established consecutive-sentence mandate, implying Congress intended both to operate simultaneously; and (4) petitioner's and the government's 'double-language requirement' — demanding both statutes contain cumulative-punishment language — is unsupported by precedent and inconsistent with statutory history.

Blockburger v. United States — foundational lesser-included offense test used to determine whether two offenses are the 'same offense' for Double Jeopardy purposes
Delligatti v. United States, No. 23-825 — pending Supreme Court case on 'crime of violence' definition under § 924(c), cited as potentially clarifying governing legal principles relevant to this case

case_analysis.legal_complexity: Complex — This case involves the intersection of multiple layers of statutory interpretation, Double Jeopardy doctrine, lesser-included offense analysis, and structural congressional intent analysis. The unusual posture — where the United States (Solicitor General) supports the petitioner against its own prior litigation position and a Court-appointed amicus defends the judgment below — adds procedural and jurisprudential complexity. Additionally, the potential interplay with the pending Delligatti decision and the long procedural history of the case (spanning multiple Second Circuit appeals and a prior certiorari petition) further elevates its complexity.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Alito continue to press the strongest counterargument — that § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)'s consecutive-sentencing mandate operates as structural backdrop sufficient under Missouri v. Hunter without requiring restatement in § 924(j). But as I noted in my prior reasoning, and as Justice Gorsuch articulates most precisely, this argument proves too much: it would render the Blockburger presumption a nullity whenever Congress builds a new offense on an existing penalty framework, because the prior statute's consecutive-sentencing command would always supply the requisite clarity. What distinguishes this case from Hunter is that Congress demonstrated within § 924(c) itself — through selective deployment of explicit cumulative-punishment language for certain predicates — that it knows exactly how to authorize stacking, and its failure to employ that same language in § 924(j) is not mere silence but an affirmative drafting signal. As Chief Justice, I would assign a narrow opinion confined to the specific § 924(c)/§ 924(j) pairing, explicitly preserving Hunter's broader framework and declining to hold that structural backdrop can never supply legislative intent — a minimalist holding that should hold the 7-justice majority without unnecessarily disturbing the broader double jeopardy landscape or inviting challenges to other statutory configurations.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: After careful reflection on Justice Gorsuch's and Justice Barrett's arguments, I find myself persuaded by a point I had not fully credited: the selective deployment of cumulative-punishment language within § 924(c) itself is not merely an absence of language in § 924(j) but an affirmative textual signal under the expressio unius canon. As a textualist and originalist, I cannot dismiss this as mere drafting oversight when Congress demonstrably knew how to authorize stacking and chose not to replicate that authorization in § 924(j). Justice Alito's structural backdrop argument — which mirrors my own prior reasoning — ultimately does prove too much, because it would render the Blockburger presumption a nullity whenever a new offense is enacted within an existing penalty framework, and Missouri v. Hunter's requirement of 'clear' legislative intent cannot be satisfied by inference alone when the text affirmatively signals the opposite. I therefore join the majority, though I write separately to emphasize that this holding is narrow and does not disturb Hunter's framework where Congress has genuinely authorized cumulative punishment through structural design rather than selective omission.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Gorsuch's expressio unius argument remains the most formidable challenge to my position, and I acknowledge that seven colleagues find it persuasive — but I cannot accept the premise that Congress's use of 'in addition to' language within § 924(c)(1)(A) for predicate offenses carries a negative implication for the entirely different structural relationship between § 924(c) and § 924(j). The 'in addition to' language in § 924(c)(1)(A) addresses stacking the firearms offense on top of the underlying predicate crime of violence or drug trafficking — a horizontal relationship between distinct offenses — whereas the § 924(c)/§ 924(j) relationship is vertical, with § 924(j) being an aggravated form of § 924(c) itself; these are categorically different drafting contexts, and the canon of expressio unius requires that the omitted item be from the same class as the included items. Justice Barrett's textualist methodology, which I generally share, leads her to conclude that selective deployment of stacking language is dispositive, but I would note that Missouri v. Hunter's framework was designed precisely to avoid requiring magic words in every statute when the overall scheme clearly authorizes cumulative punishment — and § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)'s mandatory consecutive command was operative law when § 924(j) was enacted, making it the more natural source of authorization. I maintain my position, though with reduced confidence given the weight of my colleagues' collective reasoning, because I believe the majority has not adequately distinguished between the absence of explicit authorization and the presence of implicit authorization through pre-existing statutory architecture.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas's structural backdrop argument remains the most serious challenge to my position, but after careful reflection it still fails for the reason Justice Gorsuch identifies with precision: Missouri v. Hunter requires affirmative clarity, not inference from pre-existing statutory architecture, and when Congress selectively deployed explicit cumulative-punishment language within § 924(c) for specific predicate relationships while enacting § 924(j) in complete silence, that contrast is not mere drafting economy but a meaningful textual signal under the canon against surplusage and expressio unius. Justice Alito's practical concern about anomalous sentencing outcomes — that murder-by-firearm would carry less cumulative exposure than non-lethal firearm offenses — has genuine intuitive force, but as Justice Gorsuch correctly notes, § 924(j) already carries life imprisonment or death, meaning the aggravated offense itself imposes greater punishment and the 'superseding offense' model resolves the anomaly without requiring courts to infer stacking authorization that Congress never wrote. The rule of lenity provides the decisive tiebreaker here: where the government's own Solicitor General has abandoned the prior litigation position and the structural inference is genuinely contested among careful jurists, that ambiguity must resolve in favor of the defendant — the Double Jeopardy Clause demands no less before we impose what is functionally double punishment for the same underlying firearm conduct. I remain firmly with the Petitioner.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas's structural argument — that § 924(c)(1)(D)(ii)'s consecutive-sentencing mandate operates as the operative backdrop authorization under Missouri v. Hunter — remains the most serious challenge to my position, but I find it ultimately unpersuasive for reasons that have only sharpened through deliberation.
